title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: We spent a few sad hours until eleven o'clock, when the trial was set to begin. My father and the rest of the family had to attend as witnesses, so I went with them to the court. Throughout this wretched mockery of justice, I suffered living torture. The verdict would decide whether my curiosity and reckless experiments would cause the death of two people: one an innocent, smiling baby, the other far more cruelly murdered, with every added disgrace that could make a murder memorable in its horror. Justine was a girl of merit whose qualities promised a happy life. Now everything was to be destroyed in a shameful grave — and I was the cause! A thousand times I would rather have confessed to the crime myself. But I'd been absent when it happened. Such a declaration would be dismissed as the ravings of a madman and wouldn't clear Justine, who was suffering because of me.

Justine appeared calm. She wore mourning, and her face — always appealing — was made exquisitely beautiful by the depth of her feelings. Yet she seemed confident in her innocence and didn't tremble, though thousands stared at her with hatred. All the sympathy her beauty might have aroused was destroyed by the spectators' imagining of the monstrous crime she supposedly committed. She was composed, though her composure was clearly forced. Her earlier confusion had already been cited as proof of guilt, so she steeled her mind to show courage. When she entered the court, she looked around and quickly found where we were sitting. A tear seemed to dim her eye when she saw us, but she quickly recovered. A look of sorrowful affection seemed to declare her complete innocence.

The trial began. After the prosecutor stated the charge, several witnesses were called. Several strange facts combined against her — enough to have shaken anyone who didn't have the proof of her innocence that I had. She had been out all night on the night of the murder. Toward morning, she'd been spotted by a market woman near where the body was later found. When asked what she was doing there, she looked strange and gave a confused, unintelligible answer. She returned to the house around eight o'clock. When someone asked where she'd been all night, she said she'd been looking for the child and urgently asked if there was any news of him. When shown the body, she fell into violent fits and was bedridden for several days. Then the miniature portrait was produced — the one the servant found in her pocket. When Elizabeth, in a faltering voice, confirmed it was the same picture she'd hung around William's neck an hour before he disappeared, a murmur of horror and outrage filled the courtroom.

Justine was called to defend herself. As the trial progressed, her expression had changed. Surprise, horror, and misery were written on her face. Sometimes she fought back tears. But when asked to plead, she gathered her strength and spoke in an audible, though unsteady, voice.

"God knows," she said, "how completely innocent I am. But I don't expect my protests alone to clear me. I rest my innocence on a plain and simple explanation of the facts that have been presented against me. I hope the character I've always maintained will lead my judges to interpret any doubtful or suspicious circumstances in my favor."

She then explained that she had spent the evening of the murder at the house of an aunt in Chêne, a village about three miles from Geneva, with Elizabeth's permission. On her way back, around nine o'clock, she met a man who asked if she'd seen a lost child. Alarmed, she spent several hours searching for him. When the city gates were shut, she was forced to spend the night in a barn, unwilling to disturb the cottage owners, who knew her well. She spent most of the night awake there. Toward morning she believed she slept a few minutes before being woken by footsteps. At dawn she left her shelter to search again. If she'd gone near the spot where his body lay, she didn't know it. Her confusion when questioned by the market woman wasn't surprising — she'd had a sleepless night, and William's fate was still unknown. As for the portrait, she had no explanation.

"I know," the unhappy victim continued, "how heavily this one piece of evidence weighs against me. But I have no way to explain it. When I've declared my complete ignorance, all I can do is guess how it might have been placed in my pocket. But even here I'm stuck. I believe I have no enemy on earth. Surely no one would try to destroy me for no reason. Did the murderer put it there? I know of no chance he would have had. And even if he did, why would he steal the jewel only to immediately give it away?

"I place my fate in the hands of my judges. Yet I see no reason for hope. I ask permission to have a few witnesses speak to my character. If their testimony can't outweigh my supposed guilt, then I must be condemned — though I would stake my salvation on my innocence."

Several witnesses who had known her for years were called, and they spoke well of her. But fear and hatred of the crime they supposed her guilty of made them timid and reluctant to come forward. Elizabeth saw even this last hope — Justine's excellent character and spotless record — about to fail her. Although deeply shaken, she asked permission to address the court.

"I am," she said, "the cousin of the murdered child — or rather his sister, for I was raised by his parents and have lived with them since long before his birth. It may seem improper for me to speak at this trial. But when I see a fellow human being about to die through the cowardice of her supposed friends, I must speak up and say what I know of her character. I know the accused well. I lived in the same house with her — for five years at one time and nearly two years at another. During all that time she seemed to me the most kind and generous person imaginable. She nursed my aunt, Madame Frankenstein, in her final illness with the greatest love and care. Afterward she nursed her own mother through a long illness in a way that inspired everyone's admiration. Then she lived again in my uncle's house, where every member of the family loved her. She was warmly devoted to the child who is now dead and treated him like the most affectionate mother. For my own part, I don't hesitate to say that despite all the evidence against her, I believe absolutely in her innocence. She had no reason for such an act. As for the trinket that forms the main evidence — if she had wanted it, I would gladly have given it to her. That's how much I value and respect her."

A murmur of approval followed Elizabeth's simple, powerful appeal. But it was inspired by her generous courage, not by any shift in feeling toward poor Justine. The public's rage actually turned on her with renewed force, accusing her of the darkest ingratitude. Justine herself wept as Elizabeth spoke but didn't respond. My own agitation and anguish during the entire trial were extreme. I believed in her innocence — I knew it. Could the demon who had murdered my brother — I didn't doubt it for a minute — also, in his hellish sport, have betrayed an innocent person to death and disgrace? I couldn't bear the horror of my situation. When I saw that public opinion and the judges' faces had already condemned my unhappy victim, I rushed from the courtroom in agony. The suffering of the accused didn't equal mine. She was sustained by innocence. But the fangs of remorse tore at my heart and wouldn't let go.

I spent a night of unrelieved wretchedness. In the morning I went back to the court. My lips and throat were parched. I didn't dare ask the fatal question, but the officers knew me and guessed why I was there. The votes had been cast. They were all guilty. Justine was condemned.

I can't describe what I felt then. I'd experienced horror before and tried to put it into words. But no language can convey the heartsick despair I endured. The official I spoke to added that Justine had already confessed. "That confession," he observed, "was hardly necessary in such a clear-cut case. But I'm glad of it. None of our judges likes to condemn anyone on circumstantial evidence alone, no matter how decisive."

This was strange and unexpected news. What could it mean? Had my eyes deceived me? Was I really as mad as the whole world would think if I revealed what I suspected? I hurried home. Elizabeth demanded to know the result.
"My cousin," I replied, "it's been decided as you might have expected. All judges would rather let ten innocent people suffer than let one guilty person escape. But she has confessed."

This was a devastating blow to poor Elizabeth, who had relied firmly on Justine's innocence. "Alas!" she said. "How shall I ever believe in human goodness again? Justine, whom I loved like a sister — how could she have worn that mask of innocence only to betray us? Her gentle eyes seemed incapable of cruelty or deceit, yet she's committed murder."

Soon we heard that the poor victim had asked to see my cousin. My father urged Elizabeth not to go, but left it to her own judgment. "Yes," said Elizabeth, "I'll go, even though she's guilty. And you, Victor, must come with me. I can't go alone." The thought of this visit was torture to me, but I couldn't refuse.

We entered the gloomy prison cell and found Justine sitting on some straw at the far end, her hands in shackles, her head resting on her knees. She stood when she saw us. When we were left alone with her, she threw herself at Elizabeth's feet, weeping bitterly. My cousin wept too.
"Oh, Justine!" she said. "Why did you rob me of my last consolation? I trusted your innocence. I was already wretched, but not as miserable as I am now."
"Do you too believe I'm so terribly wicked? Do you too join my enemies in crushing me, condemning me as a murderer?" Her voice was choked with sobs.

"Stand up, my poor girl," said Elizabeth. "Why kneel if you're innocent? I'm not your enemy. I believed you guiltless despite all the evidence, until I heard that you'd confessed your guilt yourself. You say that report is false. Be certain, dear Justine, that nothing can shake my faith in you except your own confession."

"I did confess — but I confessed a lie. I confessed to obtain absolution. But now that falsehood weighs on my heart more heavily than all my other sins. God in heaven forgive me! Ever since I was condemned, my confessor has pressured me relentlessly. He threatened and terrorized me until I almost started to believe I was the monster he said I was. He threatened excommunication and hellfire in my last moments if I didn't give in. Dear lady, I had no one to support me. Everyone looked on me as a wretch doomed to shame and damnation. What could I do? In a weak moment I agreed to a lie. Only now am I truly miserable."

She paused, weeping, then continued, "I thought with horror, my sweet lady, that you might believe your Justine — whom your blessed aunt honored so highly, and whom you loved — was capable of a crime only the devil himself could commit. Dear William! Dearest blessed child! I'll see you again soon in heaven, where we'll all be happy. That thought consoles me, even as I go to face disgrace and death."

"Oh, Justine! Forgive me for doubting you, even for a moment. Why did you confess? But don't grieve, dear girl. Don't be afraid. I'll proclaim your innocence. I'll prove it. I'll melt the stony hearts of your enemies with my tears and prayers. You shall not die! You — my playmate, my companion, my sister — you won't die on the scaffold! No! No! I could never survive such a horror."

Justine shook her head sadly. "I'm not afraid to die," she said. "That terror has passed. God gives me strength to endure the worst. I'm leaving a sad and bitter world. If you remember me and think of me as someone unjustly condemned, I accept my fate. Learn from me, dear lady, to submit with patience to heaven's will."

During this conversation, I'd retreated to a corner of the cell to hide the horrible anguish consuming me. Despair! Who dared speak of that? The poor victim, who would cross the terrible boundary between life and death tomorrow, didn't feel the deep, bitter agony I felt. I ground my teeth together and groaned from the depths of my soul. Justine started at the sound. When she saw who it was, she approached me and said, "Dear sir, you're very kind to visit me. I hope you don't believe I'm guilty?"
I couldn't answer. "No, Justine," said Elizabeth. "He's even more convinced of your innocence than I was. Even when he heard you'd confessed, he didn't believe it."

"I truly thank him. In these last moments, I feel the sincerest gratitude toward those who think of me with kindness. How sweet is others' affection to a wretch like me! It takes away more than half my misery. I feel as if I could die in peace now that you, dear lady, and your cousin believe I'm innocent."

So the poor victim tried to comfort others and herself. She did achieve the resignation she sought. But I — the true murderer — felt the never-dying worm alive in my heart, allowing no hope or consolation. Elizabeth also wept and was unhappy, but hers was the misery of innocence — like a cloud passing over the fair moon, temporarily hiding but never dimming its brightness. Anguish and despair had penetrated to the core of my heart. I bore a hell within me that nothing could extinguish. We stayed several hours with Justine. Elizabeth could barely tear herself away. "I wish," she cried, "that I could die with you. I can't live in this world of misery."

Justine put on an air of cheerfulness while struggling to hold back her bitter tears. She embraced Elizabeth and said, in a voice of barely controlled emotion, "Farewell, sweet lady, dearest Elizabeth, my beloved and only friend. May heaven bless and preserve you. May this be the last misfortune you ever suffer! Live, and be happy, and make others happy too."

The next day, Justine died. Elizabeth's heartbreaking eloquence failed to move the judges from their settled belief that this saintly sufferer was guilty. My passionate, indignant protests were ignored. When I heard their cold replies and their harsh, unfeeling logic, the confession I'd been about to make died on my lips. I could have proclaimed myself a madman, but I could not have undone the sentence passed on my wretched victim. She died on the scaffold, branded as a murderess.

From the tortures of my own heart, I turned to watch Elizabeth's deep, silent grief. This too was my doing! And my father's suffering, and the ruin of our once-happy home — all were the work of my thrice-cursed hands! You weep, unhappy ones, but these are not your last tears! You'll raise the funeral cry again and again! Frankenstein — your son, your kinsman, your early and dearly loved friend, who would give every drop of his blood for you, who has no thought of joy except as reflected in your dear faces, who would fill the air with blessings and spend his life serving you — he tells you to weep, to shed countless tears. He would be happy beyond his hopes if this could satisfy inexorable fate, and if destruction would pause before the peace of the grave replaces your sad torment!
So spoke my prophetic soul, as, torn by remorse, horror, and despair, I watched those I loved grieve helplessly over the graves of William and Justine, the first victims of my unholy experiments.
